newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Economists see RBNZ seen approving easing to date.
newsitem.headline: Economists see RBNZ seen approving easing to date.

text.p: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand is widely expected to give its stamp of approval to a recent market-led easing when it releases its monetary policy statement (MPS) next week, economists said on Friday.

Short-term interest rates fell half a percentage point to around 7.9 percent and the New Zealand dollar dipped on Tuesday's news that the New Zealand First Party had joined a coalition with the inumbent conservative National Party.

Economists said the rally changed the outlook for the MPS, due on Tuesday. They had previously predicted an official easing in monetary conditions, but the market beat the bank to it. Commentators now expect the RBNZ to sanction the move lower which has already taken place.
"There is even the possibility of a bit more (easing), I think. You can't rule it out completely," said Bank of New Zealand economist Peter Jolly.

He said given the new government's widening of the central bank's underlying inflation target band to 0-3 percent from 0-2 percent, monetary conditions were still slightly tighter than they needed to be.

The RBNZ would be happy to see the market take 90-day bill rates as low as 7.75 percent, Jolly suggested. The bank would not officially signal this further easing, however, in case the market ran too far.
Bankers Trust chief economist David Plank said the RBNZ would be reluctant to allow conditions to ease further until it had seen December quarter inflation data, due on January 17.

ASB economist Anthony Byett was a little surprised rates had already dropped as low as they had, but said it probably reflected the rise in the mid-point of the inflation target band to 1.5 percent from one percent.

"The fact that they (the RBNZ) have allowed conditions to ease this week suggests there's not that commitment to try and get a one percent year-ahead inflation rate -- that they would make do with a 1.5," he said.
Byett said the policies of the new coalition government, which include higher spending as well as the wider inflation band, had changed the inflation profile for the next few years.
"If you asked what's the average inflation rate over the next five years, I'd have to say it's probably half to one percent higher than what I would have said a week ago."
NZ First leader Winston Peters' role as Treasurer was another factor in that prediction, Byett said. The new position is the top finance job, with the finance minister next in line.

"I don't think he will be as tight, as frugal, as previous finance ministers. Peters seems to be a populist and people come to him lobbying. I suspect he will succumb to some of those lobby groups...I just think the system will get orientated towards slippage all the way through, and they're not going to
have that concern to keep inflation down," Byett said.
National Bank economist Kevin Smit said the wider target band and easier fiscal policy would probably not materially alter the inflation track on a 12-18 month view.

"But there are some risks once you get beyond that period...the fiscal policy stance gets noticeably more lax from July 1998, and there are some risks that even before then there could be some slippage," Smit said.
He said the wider target band could also add upside risk to the medium-term outlook for inflation, as people's behaviour could change if they expected average inflation would be higher.
Economists were uncertain how Tuesday's MPS, written before the new government was formed, would tackle the issue of updating RBNZ forecasts.
